rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author opens the book with al-Fatiha for blessing.
rows.anchor: نفتتح الكتاب بسورة الفاتحة تَبَرُّكاً.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamd is praise of beauty, whether a quality or gift, with love and reverence.
rows.anchor: معنى {الحمد} : الثناءُ على الجميل من نعمةٍ أو غيرها مع المحبة والإجلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamd covers praise of intrinsic qualities and beneficence, and is directed only to a living, rational being.
rows.anchor: ولا يكون {الحمد} إلا للحَيِّ العاقل

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Madḥ is broader than hamd because one may praise beautiful pearls or jewels, but cannot give them hamd.
rows.anchor: جاء في تفسير الرازي: "إن المدحَ قد يحصل للحي ولغير الحي

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One distinction says hamd follows a real benefaction or praiseworthy quality, while madḥ may precede any good deed or be undeserved.
rows.anchor: إن المدحَ قد يكون قبل الإحسان، وقد يكون بعده، أما الحمد فإنه لا يكونُ إلا بعد الإحسان

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet warns against excessive flatterers, supporting the distinction between deserved hamd and potentially misplaced madḥ.
rows.anchor: فقد قال صلى الله عليه وسلم: "احثُوا الترابَ في وجوه المَدَّاحين"

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet says that whoever does not praise people has not praised God, recognizing gratitude for people's real contributions.
rows.anchor: في حين قال: "مَنْ لم يَحمدِ الناسَ لم يحمدِ الله"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-hamd lillah implies that God is living, possesses perfect qualities, and does beautiful deeds and favors; madḥ lillah would not convey all this.
rows.anchor: علمنا من قوله: {الحمد للَّهِ} أنَّ الله حَيٌّ، له الصفات الحسنى والفعل الجميل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamd includes love, exaltation, and reverence beyond madḥ, making hamd the more fitting choice.
rows.anchor: في الحمد تعظيماً وإجلالاً ومحبة، ما ليس في المدح

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Hamd applies whether a favor reaches the speaker or someone else, whereas shukr is limited to a favor received by the speaker.
rows.anchor: إن الحمد يعمُّ ما إذا وصل ذلك الإنعامُ إليكَ أو إلى غيرك، وأما الشكر، فهو مختصٌّ بالإنعام الواصل إليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One thanks a person only for a benefit received, but may praise that person's benefit to oneself or others.
rows.anchor: فأنتَ تشكر الشخص إذا أوصلَ إليك نعمةً، وأما الحمدُ فإنه لا يختص بذاك

rows.speaker: لسان العرب
rows.claim: Hamd is more general than shukr: one praises intrinsic qualities and gifts, but does not thank someone for an intrinsic quality.
rows.anchor: جاء في (لسان العرب) : "والحمد والشكر متقاربان والحمدُ أعمّهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamd is preferable to both madḥ and shukr because it covers God's qualities and favors to the speaker and all creation.
rows.anchor: فكان اختيار (الحمد) أولى من المدح والشكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The impersonal formula al-hamd lillah does not bind praise to a particular speaker, unlike I or we praise God, and presents God as universally praised.
rows.anchor: في حين أن عبارة {الحمد للَّهِ} لا تختص بفاعل معين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying I praise God reports the speaker's act but does not establish that its object deserves praise; al-hamd lillah states God's entitlement without a specific speaker.
rows.anchor: إذا قلت: أحمد الله، أخبرتَ عن فعلك، ولا يعني ذلك أنَّ مَنْ تحمده يستحقُّ الحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb form is time-bound to the speaker's present or future, while al-hamd lillah leaves praise ongoing without a temporal limit.
rows.anchor: عبارة: {الحمد للَّهِ} مُطلقة غير مقيدة بزمن معين، ولا بفاعل معين

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: The formula means God was praised before any praiser or thanker and remains praised from eternity to eternity.
rows.anchor: جاء في (تفسير الرازي) : "إنه لو قال: (أحمدُ الله) ، أفاد ذلك كون ذلك القائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nominal sentence conveys established, lasting praise more strongly than a verbal sentence that suggests occurrence and renewal.
rows.anchor: الجملة الاسمية دالة على الثبوت، كما هو معلوم، وهي أقوى وأدوم من الفعلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-hamd lillah declares praise to be God's due by His very essence and abundant favors, unlike a report that one person praises Him.
rows.anchor: ومنها: "أن قولنا: {الحمد للَّهِ} معناه: أن الحمد والثناء حقٌّ لله وملكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamd is an inward recognition of a benefactor's favor and right to reverence; claiming I praise God can be false if the heart lacks that recognition, while the formula states a fact.
rows.anchor: الحمدَ عبارة عن صفة القلب، وهي اعتقاد كون ذلك المحمود مُتفضِّلاً منعماً مستحقاً للتعظيم والإجلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast resembles the claim of testimony: one may lie about witnessing, as the hypocrites do, but the proposition that God alone is God remains true.
rows.anchor: ولهذا قال تعالى في تكذيب المنافقين: {والله يَشْهَدُ إِنَّ المنافقين لَكَاذِبُونَ}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nominative reading al-hamdu makes a nominal sentence and is stronger and more enduring than the accusative, which requires an implied verb.
rows.anchor: قراءة الرفع تدل على أن الجملة اسمية، في حين أن قراءة النصب، تدل على أن الجملة فعليه

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: The nominative shift signals a settled meaning; the raised salam in Abraham's reply indicates a more enduring and complete greeting than theirs.
rows.anchor: جاء في (الكشاف) : "والعدل بها عن النصب إلى الرفع على الابتداء

rows.speaker: البحر المحيط
rows.claim: The seven readers agree on the nominative, which establishes praise; the accusative requires an implied agent and makes praise actor-specific and renewed.
rows.anchor: وجاء في (البحر المحيط) : "وقراءة الرفع أمكن في المعنى، ولهذا أجمع عليها السبعةُ

rows.speaker: البيضاوي
rows.claim: The nominative is chosen to convey praise's universality and permanence rather than a renewed event.
rows.anchor: وجاء في (تفسير البيضاوي) : "وإنما عدل عنه إلى الرفع، ليدلَّ على عموم الحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the accusative is read as an imperative, commanding praise does not establish that the praised one deserves it; the nominative indicates deserved, established praise.
rows.anchor: الأمر بالشيء، لا يعني أن المأمور به مستحق للفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-hamdu lillah is a nominal and definite expression, unlike hamdan lillah; al can indicate known praise or all praise, while indefiniteness lacks this scope.
rows.anchor: وإن (الحمد) مُعَرَّفةٌ بأل في حين أن (حمداً) نكرة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take al as referring to the familiar praise among people, while others read it as encompassing every instance and kind of praise.
rows.anchor: سبيل الاستغراق، فيدل على استغراق الأحمدة كلها. وَرجَّحَ بعضهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers both senses together: familiar praise belongs to God in a way that encompasses every kind and instance.
rows.anchor: والراجحُ فيما يبدو لي، أن المعنيين مرادان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most scholars treat al-hamd lillah as a report that praise is established for God; others call it performative praise, a transferred report, or a report that entails performance, and the author accepts both report and exaltation.
rows.anchor: وهذا هو الراجح في رأيي، فإنها تحتمل الخبر وإنشاء التعظيم، فتجمع المعنيين معاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-hamd lillah is better than inna al-hamd lillah because believers do not doubt the claim, and the unmarked formula can report praise while enacting exaltation; inna makes it mere report.
rows.anchor: إن عبارة: (الحمد لله) ، تحتمل الخبر وإنشاء التعظيم كما ذكرنا فتجمع المعنيين معاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-hamd lillah is better than lillah al-hamd here: fronting lillah suggests exclusivity or rebuttal of doubt, neither of which fits this address to believers.
rows.anchor: إن المقامَ ليس مقام إزالة شك، ولا أنَّ هناك من ادّعى أن الحمد لغير الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People may rightly praise others for favors; the hadith recognizes others' merit, while 3:188 condemns seeking praise for deeds not done.
rows.anchor: فإن حُمِدُوا بما فَعلوا، فلا بأس في ذلك

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-hamd may appear to apply to God or another, so naming God clarifies it; worship can only be for God, so fronting You in 1:5 prevents an implication of worshipping another.
rows.anchor: جاء في تفسير الرازي ذِكْرُ الفرقِ بين قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Word order varies with context: al-Jathiya foregrounds God as deserving praise because it confronts disbelievers' false beliefs and denials of His lordship.
rows.anchor: وإنما يكون ذلك بحسب المقام، فإذا اقتضى المقامُ التقديمَ، قُدِّمَ وإلا فلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Jathiya answers denials of God's creative and beneficent lordship by showing Him as sole creator and provider, so He alone deserves praise; al-Fatiha addresses believers who seek steadfast guidance.
rows.anchor: فهو وحده المتفضل على وجه الحقيقة، وهو المستحق الحمد على جهة الحصر والقصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Jathiya repeatedly uses restrictive constructions, matching its context of disbelievers who reject God and setting up its exclusive praise formula.
rows.anchor: هذا من ناحية، ومن ناحية أخرى، إنَّ جُلَّ التعبيرات في سورة الجاثية، جرت على طريقة الحصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The many restrictive statements throughout al-Jathiya culminate in exclusive praise and sovereignty for God, so its context calls for fronting Him as the one deserving praise.
rows.anchor: فاقتضى المقام تقديم الذات، المستحقة للحمد من كل ناحية في سورة الجاثية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using God's proper name rather than an attribute avoids implying that He deserves praise only for one quality; the name points to His essence and entitlement across all attributes.
rows.anchor: فجاء بالذات ليدل على أن الحمد إنما استحقه لذاته هو، لا بوصفٍ دون وصف

rows.speaker: روح المعاني
rows.claim: The proper name makes God's essence, rather than one particular quality, the ground of His right to praise.
rows.anchor: جاء في (روح المعاني) : "أتى باسم الذات في الحمدلةِ لئلا يتوهم لو اقتصر على الصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allah suits the following worship verse: on the prevalent etymology it derives from ilah, the worshipped, and the Qur'an often pairs this name with worship.
rows.anchor: لأن هذا اللفظ على أشهر الأقوال مأخوذ من لفظ (الإله)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even attributes such as Living or Knowing can describe others, and even unique descriptions may not explicitly identify God, so Allah is the clearest name.
rows.anchor: لم يفهم أن المقصود به الله صراحة، فكان ذكر (الله) أولى من ذكر أي اسم آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's wording is preferable to the alternatives madḥ, shukr, I/we praise, an imperative, accusative praise, an indefinite praise, inna, fronted lillah, or a divine attribute.
rows.anchor: فتبين من هذا أن: {الحمد للَّهِ} أَوْلى من

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb can mean owner, master, educator, guardian, and benefactor; the Lord of the worlds embodies these roles.
rows.anchor: الربُّ: المالك، والسيد، والمربّي والقيّم، والمنعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An owner, master, and beneficent educator has a stronger claim to praise, and the Lord can direct His subjects as He wills.
rows.anchor: وبُدئ بالرب، لأنه له التصرف في المَسُود والمملوك والعابد بما أراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb al-alamin subsumes many divine qualities, since each name or attribute governs what it describes.
rows.anchor: ودخل تحت قوله: {رَبِّ العالمين} كثيرٌ من صفات الله تعالى

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some limit al-alamin to knowledgeable or morally responsible creatures, citing its use for those who receive warning and recognize signs.
rows.anchor: فرجَّح بعضهم أنها تفيد ذوي العلم خاصة، أو المُكَلَّفين من الخَلْقِ

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say al-alamin means humans, supported by Qur'anic references to men among the worlds and Israel receiving a distinction over them.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: إن العالمين هم الإنس بدليل قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view takes the plural to include every kind, since humans, animals, insects, and each species may each be called a world.
rows.anchor: وقيل: جمع العالم ليشمل كل جنس مما سُمِّيَ به

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view says each generation or age is a world, so the plural encompasses all peoples and eras.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كل قرن وكل جيل يسمى عالَماً أيضاً

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says the plural prevents al-alam from being understood only as the perceptible physical world, a common usage.
rows.anchor: وقيل: جمعه لاحتمال أن ينصرف الذهن بلفظ (العالَم) إلى هذا العالم المحسوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since usage commonly narrows al-alam to the perceptible world, its plural can ensure comprehensive scope.
rows.anchor: لإلْفِ النفس بالمحسوسات فجمع ليفيد الشمول قطعاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic uses show al-alamin can mean a generation or people of a particular time, including Israel, Mary, and the men addressed by Lot.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنه يَصحُّ إطلاقُ لفظ (العالمين) على الجيل الواحد، أو الأجيال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some restrict worlds to accountable beings, Pharaoh's question is answered by describing the Lord of the worlds, not by defining the word worlds.
rows.anchor: وقد خَصَّ هذه اللفظةَ بعضُ أهل العلم بالمكلفين خاصة، ورُدّ بقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' reply lists qualities of the Lord rather than defining al-alamin, just as calling a house's lord a merchant does not define the house.
rows.anchor: فليست كلمة (تاجر) أو (فقيه) أو (موظف) تفسيراً لـ (هذه الدار)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-awalim can include all beings, but al-alamin applies to rational beings or groups where rational creatures predominate, not to nonrational creatures alone.
rows.anchor: وإن (العالمين) لا تطلق إلا على ذوي العلم خاصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This plural suits al-Fatiha because its worship, aid, guidance, and moral categories address accountable creatures; Rabb al-alamin may mean their Lord or all creation with rational beings predominant.
rows.anchor: فكان هذا الاختيار أنسب شيء، ولو قال: رب العالم أو رب العوالم، لم يحسن هذا الحُسْنَ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb al-alamin also answers Jews who claim God is Lord only of Israel: He is Lord of all humanity and accountable creatures.
rows.anchor: فيه رداً على المغضوب عليهم، ومنهم اليهود الذين يدّعون أن الله ربُّ بني إسرائيل خاصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fatiha's concise Rabb al-alamin fits its focus on accountable creatures, whereas al-Jathiya explicitly names heaven and earth after repeatedly detailing their signs and God's rule over them.
rows.anchor: كل مقام اقتضى التعبير الوارد فيه، فقد تردَّدَ ذِكْرُ السماوات والأرض، وما فيهن أكثر من مرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Jathiya details God's lordship over humans and other living beings through creation, subjection, sustenance, and resurrection.
rows.anchor: فقد سَخَّرَ اللهُ البحرَ وما في السماوات والأرض للإنسان، وهذا من مظاهر الربوبية له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's mercy toward believers and the laws sent to humanity also display His lordship; al-Fatiha names moral classes while al-Jathiya details the wider cosmos.
rows.anchor: وذكر الشرائع التي أنزلها الله على البشر، وهذا كله من مظاهر الربوبية للعالمين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The differing formulations of Rabb al-alamin and Lord of heaven, earth, and worlds each fit the focus of their surah.
rows.anchor: فناسب كلُّ كلام موضعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Jathiya mentions God's true sovereignty because it condemns arrogant mockers, while al-Fatiha has no such context and mentions only praise.
rows.anchor: فناسب ذلك أن يذكر أن له الكبرياء في السماوات والأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other opening praises name God as creator, originator, owner of all things, or sender of scripture; each fits its surah and the openings complement one another.
rows.anchor: غير أن الملاحظ أن هذه الافتتاحات متكاملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God originates heaven and earth from nothing, creates by measuring and shaping, owns them and their contents, sustains and repairs them, and sends scripture to guide creation.
rows.anchor: فبعد أن ذكر أنه فطر السماوات والأرض وخلقها، ذكرَ أن له ما فيها أيضاً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These openings jointly describe God as originator, shaper, owner, sustainer, and guide through revealed books; Rabb al-alamin encompasses all these qualities and worlds.
rows.anchor: وقوله: {رَبِّ العالمين} عمَّ ذلك كلَّه

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Rabb highlights that creation depends on God not only when it begins but also while it continues, a dependence disputed for things in their state of persistence.
rows.anchor: جاء في (تفسير الرازي) : "أنه تعالى لم يقل: الحمد لله خالق العالمين، بل {الحمد للَّهِ رَبِّ العالمين}

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: The next four opening praise formulas describe particular aspects contained in al-Fatiha's general Rabb al-alamin.
rows.anchor: ثم إنه تعالى افتتح سوراً أربعة بعد هذه السورة بقوله: {الحمد للَّهِ}

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Anam's creation of heaven and earth, darkness, and light is one part of the wider lordship over all worlds in al-Fatiha.
rows.anchor: فالمذكور في أول سورة الأنعام كأنه قسم من أقسام ما هو مذكور في أول سورة الفاتحة

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Kahf's revelation nurtures souls with knowledge, a particular form of the general nurture expressed by Rabb al-alamin.
rows.anchor: والمقصود منه تربية الأرواح بالمعارف

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Saba's statement that all in heaven and earth belongs to God is one aspect of al-Fatiha's general praise of the Lord of the worlds.
rows.anchor: وبَيَّنَ في أول سورة سبأ أن الأشياء الحاصلة في السماوات والأرض له

rows.speaker: الرازي
rows.claim: Fatir's origination differs from Anam's creation by measure, yet both are aspects of Rabb al-alamin; Anam then mentions darkness and light, while Fatir mentions angels as messengers.
rows.anchor: والمذكور في هذه السورة كونه فاطراً لها ومحدثاً لذواتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pair of openings complement each other: Anam follows creation with light and darkness, while Fatir follows origination with the creation of spiritual messengers.
rows.anchor: ذكر بعد خَلْق السماوات والأرض، جَعْلَ الأنوار والظلمات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb al-alamin suits the request for guidance to the straight path because a nurturer's primary task is guidance, a frequent Qur'anic association.
rows.anchor: أن قوله: {رَبِّ العالمين} مناسب لقوله فيما بعد: {اهدنا الصراط المستقيم}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahman is the fa'lan form, suggesting renewed occurrence and fullness of mercy; al-Tafsir al-Qayyim compares it to being filled with anger or regret.
rows.anchor: جاء في (التفسير القيم) : "ألا ترى أنهم يقولون غضبان، للممتلىء غضباً

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahim's fa'il form marks a stable quality, so pairing Rahman and Rahim conveys mercy as both renewed and lasting; either form alone could suggest impermanence or a merely fixed quality.
rows.anchor: فجاء بالوصفين للدلالة على أن صفته الثابتة والمتجددة، هي الرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mercy after Rabb reassures worshippers and signals that every aspect of lordship should be merciful; God describes His exemplary messenger as kind and merciful to believers.
rows.anchor: وفيه إشارةٌ إلى أن المربي ينبغي أن يتحلى بالرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means owner of the Day of Recompense; both Malik and Malik (king) are mutawatir readings, and the author rejects ranking them because each carries a distinct meaning.
rows.anchor: والحق أنْ لا تفاضل ولا ترجيحَ بين القراءتين، فكلتا القراءتين متواترة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ownership can entail sale, gift, or lease, while a king cannot dispose of his subjects; ownership also entails stronger control because creatures are God's servants, not merely subjects.
rows.anchor: أن المالكيةَ سببٌ لإطلاق التصرف، فالمالك يتصرف فيما يملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Subjects may choose to leave a king's service, but a slave cannot choose to cease belonging to an owner, so ownership entails fuller control.
rows.anchor: إن الرعية يمكنهم إخراج أنفسهم عن كونهم رعية لذلك الملك

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet says every person is a shepherd accountable for those under their care, illustrating a king's duty toward subjects.
rows.anchor: قال صلى الله عليه وسلم: "كلُّكم راعٍ وكلكم مسؤولٌ عن رعيته"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A king must care for subjects but they need not serve him; a slave must serve the owner and may not act independently without permission.
rows.anchor: أما المملوك، فإنه يجب عليه خدمة المالك وأن لا يستقل بأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The owner reading gives greater hope: beyond a king's justice, the slave seeks food, clothing, mercy, nurture, reward, and paradise from the owner.
rows.anchor: إن قراءة (المالك) أرجى من قراءة (الملك)

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One argument calls Malik more praise-worthy because an owner may own rational and nonrational beings alike, while king is not used for inanimate things.
rows.anchor: قيل: إن (مالك) أمدحُ لأنه يحسن أن يضاف إلى من لا يضاف الملك إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ownership grants broader control even when the owner acts unjustly or wastefully, and others cannot take the owned person away.
rows.anchor: إن المالكية تبقى في يد المالك إذا تصرف فيما يملك بجور أو اعتداء أو سرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Malik reading suits the mercy named before and humanity’s need on Judgment Day for a caring owner.
rows.anchor: والخَلْقُ أحوجُ ما يكون آنذاك إلى مالك أمرهم

rows.speaker: روح المعاني
rows.claim: Malik is gentler toward sinners and fits the preceding mention of mercy; attaching ownership to Judgment Day softens its severity.
rows.anchor: كما يقول صاحب (روح المعاني) : "أرفقُ بالمذنبين مثلي وأنسب بما قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some say a king outranks an owner because kings are uniquely exalted, the two readings jointly convey ownership and kingship, as in Owner of Sovereignty.
rows.anchor: إنما أنزلت القراءتان لتجمعا بين معنيي المالك والملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning ownership of Judgment Day includes the present world, already covered by Rabb al-alamin, since one who judges the day owns the preceding days of action.
rows.anchor: وأن (يوم الدين) يعني: يوم الجزاء، ولا شك أن مالك يوم الجزاء، هو مالك ما قبله من أيام العمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yawm al-din suits the cadence and is more inclusive than yawm al-qiyama: din conveys recompense and all the afterlife, and may encompass earthly life too.
rows.anchor: مراعاة للفاصلة وترجيحاً للعموم، فإن الدين بمعنى الجزاء يشمل جميع أحوال القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Din gathers senses of reckoning, recompense, obedience, submission, subjugation, and the raising or manifestation of religion; yawm al-qiyama does not express these shades.
rows.anchor: فهو يوم الحساب، وهو يوم الجزاء، وهو يوم الطاعة والخضوع لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The quoted analysis adds that obedience is manifest inwardly and outwardly, while the alternative genitive relation rests on recompense and needs no omitted phrase.
rows.anchor: ظاهراً وباطناً، وجعل إضافة (يوم) للدين في الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yawm al-din better fits Rabb al-alamin and al-Fatiha's accountable people, whose categories require reckoning, recompense, obedience, and subjugation.
rows.anchor: فيومُ الدين أنسب من يوم القيامة من كل ناحية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding ownership to the day expresses ownership of everything and everyone and all events within it, a comprehensive sense like saying caliph of the age.
rows.anchor: فملكية اليوم هي ملكية لكل ما يجري ويحدث في ذلك اليوم ولكل ما في ذلك اليوم

rows.speaker: روح المعاني
rows.claim: The day is singled out because God's ownership becomes unmistakable when worldly claims end and all people come alone; God alone owns that day.
rows.anchor: جاء في (روح المعاني) : "وتخصيصُ (اليوم) بالإضافة مع أنه تعالى مالكُ وملكُ جميع الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is praiseworthy in His essence, lordship, rightly placed mercy, and ownership of Judgment Day; the sequence spans all times from eternity through the endless afterlife.
rows.anchor: وقد استغرق هذا الحمد الأزمنة كلها

rows.speaker: الجرجاني
rows.claim: Recompense encompasses every state of the afterlife through eternity.
rows.anchor: جاء في "حاشية الجرجاني على الكشاف" في قوله: {مالك يَوْمِ الدين} "فإن الجزاء يتناول جميع أحوال الآخرة إلى السرمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The praise covers time from eternity to eternity, echoed by praise in the first and last life and at the end of judgment; this fullness makes al-Fatiha worthy to be the Mother of the Book.
rows.anchor: فاستغرق الحمد الزمان كلَّه من الأزل إلى الأبد

rows.speaker: التفسير القيم
rows.claim: The names following praise show God is praiseworthy in divinity, lordship, mercy, and kingship.
rows.anchor: جاء في (التفسير القيم) : "في ذِكْرِ هذه الأسماء بعد الحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting You in both verbs restricts worship and seeking aid to God alone, as also expressed in other calls to worship and trust in God.
rows.anchor: قدم مفعولي (نعبد) و (نستعين) لقصد الاختصاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: I worship you states an act but does not exclude worshipping others; fronting You states that worship is exclusive.
rows.anchor: يفيد أنه خَصَّهُ بالإكرام فلم يُكْرِمْ أحداً غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating You explicitly restricts seeking aid to God; without repetition it could leave the aid's recipient unspecified or suggest worship and aid occur only together.
rows.anchor: في تكرير (إياك) من الاهتمام والقوة ما ليس في الحذف

rows.speaker: روح المعاني
rows.claim: The repetition emphasizes seeking aid from God, since without it the source of aid may remain unspecified; one pronoun could also imply the two acts occur only together.
rows.anchor: جاء في (روح المعاني) : "في سر تكرار (إياك) فقيل: للتخصيص على طلبِ العون منه تعالى
